Draw normally distributed data with serial correlation within clusters

Source: R/draw_ar.R
draw_normal_ar.Rd

Draws a first-order autoregressive (AR(1)) process separately inside each cluster, the error structure of a panel in which a unit's shocks persist from one period to the next. Within a cluster, rows are ordered by time; the first value is a draw from the stationary distribution and each later one is $$e_t = r e_{t-1} + \sqrt{1 - r^2} \, \sigma u_t, \quad r = \rho^{\Delta t},$$ where \(\Delta t\) is the gap in time since the unit's previous observation and \(u_t\) is standard normal. Because the process starts at its stationary distribution, every period has standard deviation sd and there is no burn-in. Two observations of the same unit \(k\) periods apart have correlation \(\rho^k\). With equally spaced periods this is the ordinary AR(1), and with gaps it is the continuous-time version, so an unbalanced panel needs no special handling. This is the process that nlme::corAR1() and nlme::corCAR1() assume.

Usage

draw_normal_ar(clusters, time, rho, mean = 0, sd = 1)

Arguments

clusters

Vector of unit IDs. Each unit gets its own independent series.

time

Vector giving each row's position in its unit's series. Numeric, a Date (read in days, so rho is the correlation from one day to the next), or character or factor values that read as numbers, which is what cross_levels produces for a level's ID. A factor is read by its labels, never by the order of its levels. A unit may not have two rows at the same time.

rho

Correlation between consecutive periods, strictly between -1 and 1. A negative rho needs whole-number gaps in time, since \(\rho^{\Delta t}\) is undefined otherwise.

mean

Mean, a scalar or one value per row. Default 0.

sd

Standard deviation of the process in every period. Default 1. This is the marginal standard deviation, the spread of the values in any one period, so changing rho changes persistence and leaves the variance alone. stats::arima.sim() takes the standard deviation of each period's new shock instead, which is sd * sqrt(1 - rho^2) here: the same number there gives a process 1 / sqrt(1 - rho^2) times wider, 2.3 times at rho = 0.9.

Value

A double vector of the same length as clusters, in the order the rows were given.

Details

The result is a latent normal variable. For a binary or count outcome with the same persistence, pass it on: as latent to draw_binary with a probit link, or as quantile_y = pnorm(e) to draw_count and the other draw_* functions. The serial correlation of the outcome is then weaker than rho, as with correlate.

The function draws persistent errors, not state dependence: a model in which \(Y_t\) depends on \(Y_{t-1}\) itself is a different model.

Examples

panel <- fabricate(
  units = declare_level(N = 50, u = rnorm(N)),
  periods = declare_level(N = 10),
  obs = cross_levels(
    .by = c("units", "periods"),
    e = draw_normal_ar(clusters = units, time = periods, rho = 0.7),
    Y = u + e
  )
)

# the lag-1 correlation of e within unit is close to 0.7
panel <- panel[order(panel$units, as.numeric(panel$periods)), ]
same_unit <- panel$units[-1] == panel$units[-nrow(panel)]
cor(panel$e[-1][same_unit], panel$e[-nrow(panel)][same_unit])
#> [1] 0.6924371
